entries.2025_5: While organizing the phonological categories of Xiang, Gan, and Yue dialects, I lacked a practical tool. I had to look up characters in one list after another and compile the results by hand in Excel. The tedious work made me feel powerless, and gave me the idea of organizing initials and finals by Middle Chinese categories.
entries.2025_6_12: I extracted initials, finals, and tones from the open character list of Hanzi Yindian and compiled the results in Excel. I was still comfortable working in spreadsheets, so I shared the results as XLSX files or Tencent Docs.
entries.2025_7_15: I realized that many dialect scholars and enthusiasts had the same need. I decided to build a website that could save time spent organizing materials and make Chinese historical phonology more accessible to beginners.

intro.title: ℹ️ About This Site
intro.description: "Dialect Pronunciation Atlas" (方音圖鑑) is an online platform focused on dialect queries and comparison and on geolinguistics. It presents the phonological layering of initials and finals at dialect locations, together with phonemic mergers and splits, in a clear and interactive way. The site integrates phonological queries, dialect comparison, phonological analysis, interactive maps, character-list processing, vocabulary and sentence data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project, character sets from historical rime books, village-data visualization, machine learning on natural-village names, and Praat acoustic analysis. It is a comprehensive dialect-research platform that continues to grow.

feature1.heading: Core Queries
feature1.subtitle: Middle Chinese, Phonetic Values, Tones, Characters
feature1.intro: The site's earliest and most central module, focusing on detailed analysis of dialect locations and on drawing geolinguistic comparison maps. It contains four subpages.

items.title: Middle Chinese
items.body: Organize readings by rime-book categories, supporting direct selection or keyboard input. Categories such as rime group, rime, division, openness, tone, initial series, initial group, and initial, together with voicing, place of articulation, and manner of articulation, can be freely combined for Middle Chinese in the Guangyun system. The rime book can also be switched; currently supported are Guangyun, the Dialect Survey Character List, Jiyun, Hongwu Zhengyun, and Old Chinese materials. Location input supports fuzzy matching across simplified and traditional Chinese as well as batch selection by region (Atlas Regions / MCPDict Regions). Results are shown in tables, with multiple readings displayed for polyphonic characters and different colors for literary and colloquial readings (red for literary, blue for colloquial, purple when the two share the same form, green for ordinary polyphony). Clicking the statistics button performs further drill-down queries (for example, when querying finals, clicking statistics shows the distribution of initials and tones). Pop-ups also allow further subdivision: clicking a phonetic value traces the source syllables, and clicking a place name shows detailed information about the dialect location. Multiple windows can be compared in parallel, with phonetic-value filtering and two display modes, Full and Primary. The map view layers phonetic values by proportion, and clicking points on the map likewise opens drill-down queries.

items.title: Phonetic Values
items.body: Analyze the rime-book sources of a specific phoneme (phonetic value), for example tracing a modern phoneme back to its Middle Chinese sources and the specific rime groups, rimes, initials, and openness classes in Guangyun. After entering a syllable and dialect locations, results are presented in tables and maps, supporting the number of characters, proportions, and example characters for each rime-book source. Computation is relatively intensive, so reducing the number of locations is recommended.

items.title: Characters
items.body: Enter Chinese characters to query readings across dialect locations and their Middle Chinese categories. Results include annotations; the map displays the geographical distribution of readings and supports coloring for literary/colloquial readings and polyphonic characters.

items.title: Tones
items.body: Query the tone values and tone classes of dialect locations. Results are presented in tables (different tone classes in different colors); the map can switch between tone classes for drawing, and clicking shows tone-class merger information. The API is lightweight, so thousands of dialect locations can be queried at the same time.

feature2.heading: Interactive Maps & Custom Data
feature2.subtitle: Dialect Map, Regional Mapping, Custom Data, Map Drawing
feature2.intro: Focused on the drawing and display of geolinguistic maps. It contains four subpages.

items.title: Dialect Map
items.body: Query results switch to a map view with one click, displaying phonetic values in proportion-based layers. Clicking a point on the map opens a drill-down query, with support for place-name labels, fullscreen, and basemap switching. It also presents dialect-comparison results together with dialect-region point maps and heatmaps. The Syllable Statistics feature can also draw isopleth maps of syllable counts.

items.title: Regional Mapping
items.body: Draw dialect maps by Atlas Regions / MCPDict Regions and explore dialect regions and their distribution from a geolinguistic perspective. Point maps are drawn by region level, with three selectable levels each; different regions use different colors, and hovering or clicking shows place names and regional information. The complete dataset can be used to draw a nationwide regional map. Heatmaps can also be drawn to explore the distribution density of dialect survey points.

items.title: Custom Data
items.body: Users can import personal fieldwork data; the data are visible only to the owner, bound to the account, and synchronized across devices. Two modes are supported: organizing by survey location (continually supplementing a single location) and organizing by dialect feature (continually adding dialect locations for one feature to conduct geolinguistic comparisons). Users can keep adding and managing personal data such as phonological features, character pronunciations, and tone values, and draw custom dialect maps.

items.title: Map Drawing
items.body: An online GIS drawing tool that can import geographical data such as administrative boundaries and rivers, and edit points, lines, polygons, and text labels by layer. Finished drawings can be exported as GeoJSON or images. It can also draw Thiessen polygons (Voronoi diagrams) from dialect data, using either site data or custom-uploaded dialect locations.

feature3.heading: Dialect Comparison
feature3.subtitle: Compare Characters, Middle Chinese, Tone Classes, Phonetic Values
feature3.intro: Designed for quickly and intuitively judging similarities and differences among dialect-point features. It contains four subpages.

items.title: Compare Characters
items.body: Enter two Chinese characters and select the dialect regions / locations to compare. Three colors—green (completely identical), yellow (partially identical), and red (completely different)—intuitively show the degree of similarity of readings across dialect locations. Fullscreen zoom and click-to-open pop-ups with detailed readings are supported. This can be used to observe the regional distribution of particular phonological phenomena, such as lateral fricatives and palatalization.

items.title: Compare Middle Chinese
items.body: Select two sets of rime-book category (phonological class) conditions, such as open Division I of the Dang rime group versus open Division II of the Jiang rime group in Middle Chinese Guangyun. Complex rime-book category combinations can be compared across dialect locations. A similarity algorithm is used: total overlap = Σ min(proportion of readings in group 1, proportion of readings in group 2). High overlap is shown in green, medium in yellow, and low in red. The algorithm is simple and intuitive, and is suitable for comparing phonological-class mergers within the same location.

items.title: Compare Tone Classes
items.body: Select two tone classes to analyze tone-class mergers across dialect locations (such as Yangshang–Yinqu and Yinru–Yangru mergers); multiple locations can be analyzed at once. Results show the locations where the classes merge, possibly merge, or are distinct, along with distribution maps.

items.title: Compare Phonetic Values
items.body: Select 2–5 dialect locations and display their actual readings side by side, presenting the correspondence of phonetic values for initials, finals, or tones for easy point-by-point comparison. Sankey diagrams present phonological-class mergers and splits.

feature4.heading: In-Depth Analysis of Individual Dialects
feature4.subtitle: Phonological Systems, Phoneme Classification, Syllable Statistics, Rime-Book Evolution
feature4.intro: Focused on a small number of dialect locations, with in-depth analysis of their phonetic features. It contains four subpages.

items.title: Phonological Systems
items.body: Enter a dialect location name to view its complete phonological table, the co-occurrence relations of initials, finals, and tones, and the dialect's homophone list, presenting initial–final–tone combinations (initial × final × tone) in table form. Literary/colloquial coloring is supported (red for literary, blue for colloquial, purple when the two share the same form, green for ordinary polyphony). Clicking a cell shows details, and fullscreen viewing is supported.

items.title: Phoneme Classification
items.body: Based on rime-book category features such as voicing, place of articulation, open/closed mouth, and rime group, users freely choose three classification dimensions to organize dialect initials, finals, and tones, performing initial, final, and tone classification as well as dialect phonological statistics, with counts and example characters for each category; clicking a cell opens details in a pop-up. For example, rows, columns, and cells can be freely combined in three dimensions: classify rows by voicing, columns by place of articulation, and cells by initial to count the occurrences of each initial value; or classify rows by open/closed mouth, columns by rime group, and cells by division to organize the number of final values.

items.title: Syllable Statistics
items.body: Count the number of syllables of a dialect location and draw charts and isopleth maps. Includes three modes: separate initial/final/tone statistics, toneless syllables, and toned syllables. Toned/toneless syllable statistics can jump to map drawing to create isopleth maps of syllable counts, intuitively showing how many syllables each place has. The separate initial/final/tone mode provides a pie chart (syllable proportions), a bar chart (number of locations where each syllable occurs), and a scatter plot (total syllables vs. corresponding number of locations; larger circles indicate more syllables), all clickable for detail pop-ups. A custom location-selection mode is supported, analyzing up to 100 locations at a time and counting the numbers of initials, finals, and tones at each location separately, with wheel navigation on the right for quick jumps. By default, data for all locations (3,000+ dialect points) are displayed.

items.title: Rime-Book Evolution Analysis
items.body: Query the rime-book evolution of a specified dialect location. Sankey diagrams, pie charts, and other forms show the modern sources and phonological-class splits of initials / finals / tones, and even the dialect's sound change, intuitively presenting merger and split trajectories. For example, view the correspondences between initials, finals, and tones and the rime groups and initials of Middle Chinese Guangyun.

feature5.heading: Vocabulary and Sentence Data
feature5.subtitle: Dialect Word Lists, Character-List Annotations, Language Preservation Vocabulary, Language Preservation Grammar, Yangchun Colloquial Vocabulary
feature5.intro: Query and manage vocabulary data. The word lists are collaboratively built by the site's users, who digitize word lists from existing studies. Public data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project is also included, covering 1,247 dialect locations, each with 1,000 vocabulary items and 50 sentences.

items.title: Dialect Word Lists
items.body: Query dialect vocabulary across the country online, comparing how the same word is expressed in different regions, including IPA and glosses. Supports searching by standard written word, dialect word, phonetic transcription, or gloss, and browsing word lists in card, map, and table modes. After applying for word-list editing permission, users can fill in dialect-location information, batch-upload dialect vocabulary, IPA readings, and glosses in the standard format, and validate the imported data. Users with editing permission can manage the word lists they submitted, edit entries and location information online, batch-replace content, and add or delete entries.

items.title: Character-List Annotations
items.body: Query the specific glosses in dialect character-list datasets. Supports searching characters and IPA by annotation, and also direct IPA search (which runs more slowly). Dialect locations can be filtered by place or region.

items.title: Language Preservation Vocabulary (1,000 Words)
items.body: Presents vocabulary data for each location from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project. Supports map, card, and table views. In map view, dialect locations are clustered when the scale is small, and specific vocabulary appears when zoomed in; the display can switch among glosses (text), speech (IPA), and place names, and each point opens a detail pop-up. Card view presents place name, vocabulary, annotation, pronunciation, and region, with search matching. Table view supports search, sorting (all columns), and pop-up filtering (multi-select / inverse selection).

items.title: Language Preservation Grammar (50 Sentences)
items.body: Presents sentence data for each location from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project. Also supports card, table, and map modes, with search by place name, text, or syllable and filtering by dialect region.

items.title: Yangchun Colloquial Vocabulary
items.body: Query colloquial words of the Yangchun dialect, including etymological characters, IPA readings, Jyutping, glosses, and example words and sentences; supports field-based filtering of the word list.

feature6.heading: Dialect Character-List Tools
feature6.subtitle: Character-List Validation, Jyutping to IPA, List Merging
feature6.intro: A practical toolkit for dialect fieldworkers, supporting various character-list processing scenarios. It contains three subpages.

items.title: Character-List Validation and Format Conversion
items.body: Upload a dialect character list to automatically detect non-single-character entries, unusual phonetic symbols, missing tones, and other issues; the tool automatically splits initials, finals, and tones and provides initial/final statistics and tone-class/tone-value statistics. Online editing is supported (editing cells, batch-editing initials and finals, batch-replacing tone values, deleting rows); download the modified file to save it. Character lists in Word and other formats can also be converted into a one-character-one-reading table format.

items.title: Jyutping to IPA
items.body: Upload a character list containing a Jyutping column and convert it to IPA according to rules. Custom conversion rules are supported and personal configurations can be stored. Conversion results can be previewed and downloaded.

items.title: Merge Character Lists
items.body: Upload a reference list (which determines the final order) plus the lists to merge. Column names are detected automatically (character columns: 单字/phrase/汉字/漢字; transcription columns: IPA/ipa/音标/音標/syllable); annotations are stored as Excel comments; multiple readings are separated by semicolons; missing characters are appended at the end. Multiple lists can be uploaded and the result downloaded.

feature7.heading: Rime-Book Character Sets
feature7.subtitle: Middle Chinese, Old Chinese, Early Modern Chinese, Cantonese Rime Books
feature7.intro: Browse the characters and annotations under each phonological category by expanding the hierarchy level by level. Seven rime books are included.

items.title: Middle Chinese
items.body: The Guangyun system, organized hierarchically by rime group / openness / division / rime / tone / voicing / initial series / initial group / initial. Guangyun annotations can be displayed, and the data can be reorganized by dimensions such as initial labels and voicing. Custom classification levels and order are supported.

items.title: Old Chinese
items.body: Organized hierarchically by tone / initial / final / rime group / initial group / /r/ medial / phonetic-series domain. Custom classification levels and order are supported.

items.title: Early Modern Chinese
items.body: Covers three rime books: Zhongyuan Yinyun, Hongwu Zhengyun, and Menggu Ziyun. Custom classification levels and order are supported.

items.title: Cantonese Rime Books
items.body: Hierarchical queries based on the Fenyun Cuoyao system. Custom classification levels and order are supported.

feature8.heading: Natural Village Data
feature8.subtitle: Guangdong Natural-Village Hierarchy, Toponym Distribution, Guangdong Village Table, Yangchun Natural Villages, Machine Learning
feature8.intro: Look up the geographical location, administrative divisions, and dialect information of natural villages, and explore the geographical distribution and naming patterns of village names.

items.title: Guangdong Natural-Village Hierarchy
items.body: Browse the Guangdong natural-village directory hierarchically by city, county, town, and other administrative levels (supporting expansion city → county → town → administrative village → natural village). Query village names, dialect distribution, and coordinates, and view villages on the map. Search is supported, with filtering by city, county, or town. Natural-village points are clustered at small scales and reveal specific village names and dialect data when zoomed in. The display can switch between village names and dialect data. Links to the map-drawing page let users draw dialect-distribution maps with Thiessen-polygon algorithms. The dialect data are based on the Quan Yue Cunqing series (manually recorded village by village by the author, mostly concentrated in western Guangdong: Yangjiang, Maoming, Yunfu, etc.).

items.title: Toponym Distribution
items.body: (In development) Query the distribution of Chinese characters in natural-village toponyms and explore regional toponym patterns and characteristics.

items.title: Raw Data Table
items.body: Display raw natural-village data for Guangdong Province in table form, with filtering and search matching. Filter by village name, administrative division, or dialect, view coordinates, and sort and paginate the table.

items.title: Yangchun Natural Villages
items.body: The author specially compiled and proofread the natural-village data in the Yangchun County Gazetteer (1996), using etymological characters rather than homophonous substitutes; it is more accurate than the Quan Yue Cunqing data and loads faster. Expand by administrative levels such as town and community to view the affiliation between villages and village committees.

items.title: Machine Learning Analysis (VillagesML)
items.body: A complete standalone sub-application containing seven modules and 28 analysis tabs: Character Analysis (frequency tendencies, embedding similarity, character networks, significance); Semantic Analysis (category labels, combination patterns, N-gram analysis, semantic indices, semantic networks, subcategory analysis); Spatial Analysis (spatial hotspots, spatial clustering, spatial visualization, spatial integration); Pattern Analysis (frequency analysis, structural analysis, tendency analysis, N-gram exploration, N-gram statistics); Regional Analysis (aggregate statistics, feature vectors, category tendencies, similarity analysis); ML Computation (basic clustering, character tendencies, sampled villages, spatially aware clustering, hierarchical clustering, feature extraction, subset analysis); and Search.

feature9.heading: Web-Based Praat Acoustic Analysis
feature9.subtitle: Pitch, Formants, Vowel Space, F0-Based Tone Estimation
feature9.intro: Praat's core algorithms are integrated into the backend through praat-parselmouth, so acoustic analysis can be performed directly in the browser without installing additional software. Login is required because the algorithms are CPU-intensive and server resources are limited.

items.title: Audio Upload and Trimming
items.body: Supports drag-and-drop uploads in WAV, MP3, M4A, WebM, OGG, FLAC, AAC, and other formats, as well as direct recording on the site. After recording, users can drag to select and trim segments without separate editing software. Mobile devices are supported; phone recording is recommended because it often provides better audio quality than a computer microphone.

items.title: Two Analysis Modes
items.body: Single-syllable mode precisely isolates one syllable and is best suited to vowel-space analysis. Continuous-speech mode performs automatic segmentation on the backend and may introduce some error, but it is useful for F0-based tone estimation: multiple tone classes can be uploaded together to generate a five-level tone chart using Shi Feng's T-value method.

items.title: Seven Analysis Modules
items.body: Basic information (audio duration and sampling rate); F0 analysis (tone-value features, five-level tone calculation, F0 curve); intensity analysis (mean intensity, intensity range, intensity trajectory); formant analysis (formant trajectories); voice-quality analysis (harmonics-to-noise ratio, jitter, shimmer); segment analysis (single syllable → rime_core + syllable_like; continuous speech → voiced / speech / silence); spectrogram analysis (frequency–time energy distribution, limited to audio no longer than three seconds).

items.title: Precision
items.body: Three modes are available: Fast, Standard, and High Precision.

items.title: Vowel Space
items.body: Displays vowel values and their movement trajectories. For best results, use single-syllable mode in a quiet environment and trim the segment precisely. For example, the vowel in the Yangchun Cantonese reading of 「你」 can be seen moving from ɛ down toward æ and then upward toward ɨ.

items.title: F0-Based Tone Estimation
items.body: Extract the voiced or rime_core portion of each tone class, add the segments to a list, and generate a five-level tone chart using Shi Feng's T-value method. Results can be exported to Excel. Multiple tone classes may be extracted from a single recording, and the workflow is also convenient on mobile devices.

reflection.title: 🧑‍💻 Reflections
reflection.paragraph1: It began simply as a convenience for my own research: I wrote a few Python scripts to process dialect data. Later, I organized them into a FastAPI backend and built a modest single-page interface with vanilla JavaScript. My ambition at the time was uncomplicated—a tool that felt comfortable to use would have been enough. I never expected the project to keep growing until, almost without notice, a year had passed. That year brought disappointment in the postgraduate entrance examination, anxiety about employment, and the farewells of graduation. My state of mind shifted again and again, yet in the quiet of writing code I always found a small corner in which to settle myself.
reflection.paragraph2: Over that year, I gradually became acquainted with front-end development. At the beginning of 2026, I spent three months interning as a front-end developer at an internet company, and during that period I carefully rewrote the entire project in Vue. Over the following months, I added dialect comparison, character-list processing, vocabulary and sentence data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project, village-data visualization, Praat acoustic analysis, and more. Writing code was also a way of studying phonology: building a sound query workflow often required first clarifying the phonological information behind it, while a deeper understanding of phonology continually inspired new features. Technology and scholarship nourished one another, allowing the project to become steadily more complete.
reflection.paragraph3: Today, the site receives roughly 300 visits and 8,000 API calls each day. The journey from command-line scripts to an online platform has not been straightforward, but seeing people genuinely use it—and knowing that it has helped many language enthusiasts and even university researchers—makes every effort feel worthwhile. My sincere thanks go to everyone who has offered support, encouragement, or a response. If the site can save you even a little time spent searching through reference materials, it has fulfilled its purpose.
reflection.poem:
May the voices of every region live on;
May the beauty of Chinese characters always be cherished;
May the flame of civilization endure through every interaction and every moment of resonance.
